title: Shu'ayb and the scales
hookLine: Shu'ayb tells Madyan to give full measure and not cheat people of their things (7:85)
last: SALIH AND THE SHE-CAMEL — LEAVE HER TO GRAZE.

lines: A TOWN THAT RAN ON SLIVERS.
cards: A bag of chips that's mostly air. A gas pump off by a fraction. An invoice padded with an hour nobody worked.
A shop scale nudged so a kilo is a little less than a kilo. Each one is small and easy to deny, and across thousands of customers they add up to someone getting rich on a sliver from everyone.
The Qur'an tells of a whole town that ran on slivers, and of the prophet sent to them, Shu'ayb.

teach.b: Verse eighty-five: to Madyan, their brother Shu'ayb. Madyan was a trading people; many place them in northwest Arabia, near the Gulf of Aqaba.
Shu'ayb begins with the same call as Hud and Salih: worship Allah, you have no god but Him. Then, in Pickthall's words: “give full measure and full weight and wrong not mankind in their goods.”
The word for weight, mizan, is the balance scale itself. And their goods is ashya'ahum, literally their things: don't shortchange people in anything that's theirs.
Don't spread corruption in the land after it has been set right. The next verse warns them against lurking on every road to threaten travelers.

teach.h: LEAVE, OR COME BACK TO OUR WAYS.
teach.b: The town's leaders answer with an ultimatum: leave, Shu'ayb, you and everyone who believes with you, or come back to our ways. His reply is a short question: even if we hate them?
He won't go back, and he asks God to judge between them with truth. Notice what the town is defending: not only its gods, but a way of doing business that worked very well for the people at the top.

Some commentators identified Shu'ayb with the father-in-law of Musa; many disagreed, and the Qur'an doesn't say. The end of Madyan, verse ninety-one, is the earthquake again. But the warning outlived the town.

teach.h: WOE TO THOSE WHO GIVE SHORT MEASURE.
teach.b: A whole short surah, eighty-three, opens with woe to those who give short measure.
Fair weight is no footnote in this tradition. It sits right next to worship.

how: Muslim jurists treat honest weights and measures as a religious duty, and Islamic cities historically had a market inspector, the muhtasib, who checked scales; many Muslim traders cite Shu'ayb and surah eighty-three.

games.why: 'even if we hate it?' he answers, and asks God to judge between them with truth (7:88–89).

practice: Think of the places you measure something out for others: the hours on a timesheet, the change at a register, the effort on a group project, the split of a dinner bill, the slice of cake you cut for someone else.
Find one place where you've been giving a little short, picture giving it full, maybe a touch more, and notice how that feels.
